This screen explains in plain language what the app calculates and on what basis — not a copy of the flight manual, but using the same source labels as the calculation screens themselves, so you can see what\'s a certified figure and what\'s an external rule of thumb.

[AFM] and [AFM Sup 1]/[AFM Sup 11] come directly from the certified flight manual and its supplements — these are hard, certified figures. [AIC P173] is an external, non-mandatory UK CAA guideline, used only where the flight manual itself specifies nothing.

The app calculates total weight and center of gravity (CG) from the aircraft\'s empty mass plus pilot, copilot, fuel and baggage. [AFM] This is checked against the maximum take-off mass (MTOW) and the CG envelope from your own weighing report. Exceedances show as a clear warning; an underweight solo flight shows a note that trim weight may be needed.

For take-off and landing, the app interpolates the official flight-manual performance tables based on outside air temperature, pressure altitude and (for take-off) headwind. [AFM] For surface (grass, soft ground) and slope corrections, the app uses AFM figures where they exist, and otherwise recognised rules of thumb from the UK AIC P173 circular. [AIC P173] As a final step, a recommended safety margin is applied (default 1.33x for take-off, 1.43x for landing) — not a legal requirement, but a common practical convention you can adjust yourself. [AIC P173]

For towing a glider, the app uses a separate performance table from AFM Supplement 1, which classes the aircraft into weight bands based on the sailplane\'s weight and L/D ratio. [AFM Sup 1] Surface, slope and margin corrections work the same way as for a normal take-off. Since the tow table itself is only published for dry grass, asphalt, wet grass and soft ground are mathematically derived from the normal take-off table\'s own grass-runway surcharge — not a separate AFM figure, but a transparent derivation.
This app is a practical aid, not a certified EFB. The flight manual (AFM) and its supplements always remain authoritative — see \'Source documents\' for the originals.
